parole.testo: Borrowed from Jamaican Creole cah (“because”). Ultimately from English because.

parole.significato: A hairstyle worn by Rastafarians and others in which the hair is left to grow long, and twisted into matted strings.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Jamaican Creole dreadlocks, from dread (“of or relating to a dread”, adjective) (from dread (“(usually black) male member of the Rastafarian movement who wears his hair in dreadlocks”, noun), from English dread (“reverential or respectful fear; awe”), referring to the awe inspired by G
Borrowed from Jamaican Creole fahwud (“to come”), farwud, faawud, itself a respelling of English forward.

Borrowed from Jamaican Creole irie, which is perhaps from English all right. Compare a'ight. The applied context of the remark, may also allude to a corruption of the conjugation of the french verb 'rier', such that, "I am laughing", would be a parabolic inference, about 'rightness'.
Borrowed from Jamaican Creole likkle, from English little.
From Jamaican Creole mawga, derived from English meagre.

parole.significato: An untrustworthy person; a person who deliberately acts against one's interests.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Jamaican Creole pagan, from English pagan.

parole.significato: Used to express anger, annoyance or surprise.
parole.testo: 1950s. From Jamaican Creole raasclaat, from English arse + cloth. Compare English arsewipe, asswipe.
Borrowed from Jamaican Creole sekkle, from English settle.

parole.significato: A greeting, equivalent to what's up or what's happening.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Jamaican Creole wah gwan (literally “wha’ goi’ on”), a modified form of English what's going on.
